reader.title: Reported lynching of Michael Dohm
bases: The only report relays a letter saying Michael Dohm was 'lynched' in Texas for horse stealing; the report itself is doubted and gives no particulars (A1).

A single local brief relays an unseen letter saying Dohm was lynched in Texas for horse stealing, and the paper reports that men who knew him doubted the letter's genuineness (A1); no place, date, perpetrators or Texas report appears, so neither the killing nor a group of three or more is established.
Only the Wahpeton times mentions the reported lynching, at second hand and with doubts attached (A1); its later legal notice names Dohm only as a debtor (A2).

summary.text: The reported lynching of Michael Dohm was an unconfirmed account, published in Wahpeton, Dakota Territory, in June 1888, that a local man had been lynched in Texas for horse stealing.
The story rested on a letter his wife was said to have received, which the Wahpeton paper never saw and which men who knew him doubted.
Dohm, called "Mike" in the local press, appears to have lived in or near Wahpeton, in Richland County.
His race is not given in the coverage.

On 7 June 1888 the Wahpeton times reported that it had gone to see a letter said to be in the hands of Mrs. Michael Dohm, sent from Texas and telling her that her husband "was lynched there recently for horse stealing."
Mrs. Dohm was not at home, and the paper did not see the letter.
The brief gave no place in Texas, no date and no account of who carried out the reported lynching or how.
No confirmation or denial of the letter appears in the coverage, and no Texas report of the lynching was found.

In July 1888 the same paper ran a sheriff's notice that a $349 judgment had been entered for Samuel B. Aspinwall against Michael L. Dohm, and that Dohm's drills, pipe and other well tools would be sold at auction in Wahpeton on 28 July.
The notice said nothing about Dohm's whereabouts or the reported lynching.
The episode appears only as a few lines in the Wahpeton times' local column, set between notices of rooms to let and a prize calla lily.
The paper treated the letter skeptically, writing that its genuineness was "doubted by men who know Mike's methods."
In the same sentence it added that lynching was "what 'the likes o' him' might encounter, in that country," a remark that cast doubt on Dohm's character as well as on the letter.
No other white paper was found to have carried the story, and the Black-press collection does not reach back to 1888.
